method: An exposure sheet times animation by how long each drawing stays on screen. The hold is the exposure, written in frames per drawing: on ones every frame carries a new drawing, on twos the drawing changes every second frame, and so on up to twelves. Given a scene length in seconds and a whole frame rate, the frame count is the length times the rate rounded to the nearest whole frame, because a shot can only be an integer number of frames long; the drawing count is that frame count divided by the hold and rounded up, so the sheet can end with a drawing that covers fewer frames than the rest. The last hold is what remains after the earlier drawings, the drawings per second are the frame rate divided by the hold, one drawing's on-screen time is the hold divided by the rate, and the runtime is the frame count divided by the rate. The timing table lists the first twelve drawings with their frame ranges, then the final drawing whenever the sheet is longer, because the hold then simply repeats. In the other direction a drawing count times the hold gives the frames and the frames divided by the rate give the runtime exactly, with no rounding of their own. Frame rates are whole frames per second from 1 to 120 and holds run from 1 to 12 frames, so fractional and drop-frame rates such as 23.976 and 29.97 are out of scope, as are camera-move timing, audio breakdowns and shooting schedules. A scene length accepts up to three decimals from 0.001 to 3600 seconds and a drawing count runs from 1 to 100000. A length that is not a whole number of frames is reported with the exact frame count it rounds from, a short final drawing is named rather than hidden, a sheet longer than the table is said to repeat, and a hold of a whole second or more is flagged as stop-motion pacing rather than smooth animation. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Richard Williams, The Animator's Survival Kit - exposure sheets, timing charts, and the holds used for ones, twos and threes.
Harold Whitaker and John Halas, Timing for Animation - frame-by-frame timing, holds, and how a drawing count follows from running time and frame rate.
Toon Boom Harmony and Adobe Animate documentation on exposure sheets and frame-by-frame drawing timing at integer frame rates.
